messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mike is a 49-year-old plumber, married for nearly twenty years, who lives in a midsize New England town. The trauma that reshaped his life happened six years ago, during a relationship that had turned volatile. His partner at the time, Sarah, had a temper that could shift without warning. One evening, after a quiet disagreement about money—she was angry, but her voice stayed low and controlled—she snapped. She grabbed a hot pan from the stove and pressed it into his forearm. The searing pain was followed by the smell of burnt skin and fabric, a sweet, acrid odor that he can still summon without effort. He pushed her away and left the apartment that night, ending the relationship for good. But the olfactory cue embedded itself deep: any burnt smell—from a toaster, a furnace pilot light, even a neighbor’s barbecue—can now pull him back into that kitchen.

Mike’s work as a plumber puts him in constant proximity to such triggers. Last month he was repairing a water heater in a basement when the faint scorched-metal smell of a failing thermostat reached him. His chest tightened, his hands went clammy, and he set down his tools and walked out of the house without a word to the homeowner. That evening, back at home, he found himself unable to go to bed. He knew that lying down would mean the story would replay—he would see her face, hear her voice, feel the heat—so he stayed up until nearly 3 AM, scrolling through news articles, then cleaning his truck. This delay-sleep pattern has become his nightly ritual. He has come to believe that if he can just stay awake long enough, he will eventually collapse without the memory catching him.

Confrontations are another trigger. His job sometimes involves difficult customers—a landlord angry about a burst pipe, a homeowner frustrated by a bill. Even when the person is calm, the mere expression of displeasure makes Mike feel cornered. A few weeks ago, a client calmly explained that the repair had taken longer than expected and asked for a discount. Mike heard the controlled tone and his mind went blank. He agreed to the discount just to end the conversation, then drove straight home and spent the evening trying not to think about the abuse. He has learned to avoid thinking about the event entirely: when a thought threatens to surface, he focuses on a task—tightening a fitting, organizing his van—until it passes.

The site of the old apartment where the abuse occurred is a zone he refuses to enter. He drives four extra blocks to avoid that street, and once turned down a well-paying job at a building two doors down, telling his boss the job was too complex. He never explained why. His wife has noticed he is tense after work, that he stays up late, and that he rarely talks about the years before they met. She has urged him to see someone, but he always dismissed the idea, certain that if he just keeps busy and avoids his triggers, he can manage.

But the cycle has tightened. The burnt-smell encounter at work led to a night of poor sleep, which left him irritable the next day. That irritability prompted a brief, tense exchange with a coworker—another confrontation—and Mike spent the rest of the shift avoiding the man, retreating to a back shed. That night, he again delayed sleep until his wife found him at 2 AM staring at the kitchen wall. She told him she was worried, that he seemed hollowed out. He finally agreed to schedule an appointment.

What frightens Mike most is the growing conviction that the world is layered with hidden traps—a whiff of smoke, a customer’s frown—and that he is shrinking his life to avoid them. He is tired of the late nights, the detours, the silence. He hopes that talking about what happened might loosen the grip of those triggers, though he is terrified that revisiting the memory will only make it stronger.
